Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Apathy wrote:
<<Glancing at the new DCI floor rules updates, I noticed to my dismay that RtI
is now banned. Now, I realize that I haven't had much playing experience, but
I thought banning cards was something that should be reserved for Jyhad's
inbred cousin, Magic: The Unbalancing. Am I missing something here?>>

I wouldn't worry about it. There have always been a few banned cards in the
set:

-Ante cards
-Cards that used outmoded rules (Paralyze)
-Cards that simply didn't work in a tournament (Monocle and Madness of the
Bard)

As far as I can tell, RTI is the first card banned for its effect on play, but
if any card deserved it, it was RTI. There was an attempt to fix it with
unweildy errata, which apparently didn't work. Thus, the only real option was
to ban it.

I have great faith that this isn't going to set a precident of "ban
everything", as it really isn't needed. RTI was just wrong, and with the
errata, most other cards are perfectly acceptable at this point. It seems
unlikely that there will be a string of bannings.

I hesitate to open up what I sense is a very old can of worms, but why was
RtI so abusive? Yes, its hard to counter in conjunction with Day Op, and
yes it can oust your prey in one swell foop, but it seems to be fundamentally
a combo card, and therefore hard to set up and use effectively. Also not
grotesquely hard to counter, although the simplest ways seem to lean towards
DI and AI, which are rather RtI-specific and unlikely to be included in decks
not aiming to shut down RtI.

Messages.Author: Derek S. Ray
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 25 Mar 1999 00:01:50 GMT, apathy <sky...@umich.edu> wrote:

>I hesitate to open up what I sense is a very old can of worms, but why was
>RtI so abusive? Yes, its hard to counter in conjunction with Day Op, and
>yes it can oust your prey in one swell foop, but it seems to be fundamentally
>a combo card, and therefore hard to set up and use effectively. Also not
>grotesquely hard to counter, although the simplest ways seem to lean towards
>DI and AI, which are rather RtI-specific and unlikely to be included in decks
>not aiming to shut down RtI.

RtI's card text: (cost, 4 blood... largely meaningless.)

Requires a ready vampire. (D) Bleed your prey with +X bleed, where X
is the capacity of the acting vampire. Burn this vampire if this
action is successful.

The big boo-boo here is "where X is the capacity" - even Spiridonas
has to actually have the blood ON him to pull off his megableed.
Anyone else just has to have 4 blood and Fortitude - meaning you bring
out your IC member with Fortitude and superior Dominate, probably
Arika. IC members bleed for 3 to start with. +11 for Arika makes 14,
and modify the bleed with Conditioning for a bleed of 17. Day Op it.
Kaboom. Deflect or die.

That's only a 3-card combo for a bleed of 17. Add a minion tap for 6
as your master phase action, and you have bled for 17, unblockably,
using 4 cards and spending 5 pool. This is so abusive of the
carefully thought-out "cost to effect" ratio in Jyhad, it's not even
funny.

Defenses? Well, pack Deflections, but those require two things:
either dominate or superior Auspex (for Telepathic Misdirection), and
you MUST have the card in your hand. If you're a Rush deck, you can
rush Arika first and hope like hell you can pound at least 8 blood off
of her - but look out for that pesky Obedience, which I'd certainly
put in an RtI deck. Better forget combat.

Direct Intervention - neat idea, but you'll just get hit next time
around by the NEXT RtI card in the deck. That only kills one instance
of it, unfortunately - and it's a 'prayer' card, so you don't usually
include very many of them in your deck. Archon Investigation - very
neat idea, but even more of a "prayer" card since if nobody bleeds you
for more than 3, it wastes space. Much more popular while RtI was NOT
banned, but why should I HAVE to include enough of any card to ensure
drawing it in my first 10 cards just so that I will live?

Oh, there's also "have enough pool to survive the bleed". Well, Arika
just happens to have superior OBF - so you pack a few Lost in Crowds
and bleed for 6 each turn with those Conditioning modifiers that you
ALREADY HAVE IN YOUR DECK until you knock them down enough so that an
RtI ousts them. Added advantage - this has a tendency to make people
waste Deflections on smaller bleeds.

The problem here is, it IS possible to make decks that successfully
defend against bleed WITHOUT using Deflections - Animalism untap comes
to mind. Day Opping a bleed for 6 is painful to those decks, yes, but
it comes at a price - the vampire is in torpor, munch fodder, and it's
only a bleed for 6. Why should we force everyone to pack Deflections
because the guys who designed Ancient Hearts had a horribly bad idea?
=)

-- Derek

>often accused of being more interested in quirky card combos than in strategy
>[and there is a lot of truth in that accusation], but i think this time i am
>seeing the strategic point of rti better than some of you strategists!

Except it also boosted any other clan with big vampires as well as the
Nosferatu, making no significant benefit to one or the other.
(Although granted, it was one of the nicer ways the Nossies could
actually get some bleed when they got done sneaking around and
knocking your block off.)

I would almost have wished for errata saying "Bleed. This vampire may
burn X additional blood during this action to gain +X bleed.", and of
course alter that 'burn this vampire' to 'remove this vampire from the
game' to knock out potential pesky Soul Gem loops. The previous deck
would then still be able to bleed for 12, but not without it costing
them 11 pool OR the time required to Minion Tap/5th Tradition someone
first... but I'm sure there is a way to abuse that errata floating
around somewhere.
